---
title: "11. Price your own claim"
aliases:
  - /price-your-own-claim.html
---

Everything in this course so far priced the paper's three claims: the market and
the two legs of the book-to-market sort. This chapter shows you how to
price a claim of your own. Bring a dividend process, e.g., a portfolio's
dividends, a firm's distributable earnings, or any cash-flow stream you
can put a growth series to. The model then reports how the claim's
valuation responds to long-run growth news and what that exposure costs.

The contrast to remember is [Chapter 1](01-two-free-numbers.qmd). A DCF
prices a claim from two free numbers, a growth rate and a discount rate,
and nothing inside the method disciplines either one. Here the claim
brings exactly one number of its own, the loading of its cash flows on
the persistent component of consumption growth, and you measure that
number from cash flows alone. Nobody chooses the discount rate. The
household of [Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) sets it, and
the same household prices every claim. Returns never enter the
estimation, so the premium that comes out is a prediction, not a fit.

The point of building a general equilibrium model instead of a
spreadsheet is exactly the arrangement above. One economy, with one set
of preferences, prices every claim in the cross-section by where its
cash flows fall when news arrives about the next decade of growth.

## The steps

Pricing a claim takes four steps, and none of them uses a return.

1. **Obtain your claim's cash-flow growth series.** Use annual log
   dividend growth for a portfolio, or growth in distributable earnings
   for a firm. The growth series is the only input the claim
   contributes.
2. **Measure its long-run leverage.** Project the growth series on the
   two-year moving average of lagged consumption growth, as in equation
   (19) of the paper and
   [Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd). The slope is the loading
   $\tilde\phi$.
3. **Build a model from the loading and solve it.**
   `lrr.LongRunRisksModel.from_loading(phi)` embeds the claim in the
   Table II economy, and `.solve(method="analytical")` solves the
   log-linear model of [Chapter 6](06-log-linear-solution.qmd) for that
   one claim. A model with a single claim has no market leg, so market
   betas are undefined and the analytical method is the one to use.
4. **Read off the outputs.** `A1` is the elasticity of the
   price-dividend ratio to $x_t$, so it measures how the claim's
   valuation responds to growth news. `long_run_premium` is the
   annualized compensation for bearing that news, in percent.
   `gordon_return` is what a Gordon growth formula would report at the
   same anchor, using the growth channel alone with no adjustment for
   risk.

## Two synthetic firms

Before using real data, run the cleanest possible experiment. Price two
firms that are identical in every respect except the loading. Nothing is
estimated and nothing is re-tuned between the rows, so the loading is
the only difference. Both firms go into one model, so a single solve
prices the pair and the code shows the one field that changes between
them.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
# Data bootstrap: use the repo's committed CSVs, or fetch them when this
# notebook runs outside the repository.
from pathlib import Path
import urllib.request

DATA = Path("../../data")
if not DATA.exists():
    DATA = Path("data")
    DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    base = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tlorans/"
            "kiku-value-premium-replication/main/data/")
    for f in ("annual_panel.csv", "consumption_annual.csv", "rf_annual.csv"):
        if not (DATA / f).exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + f, DATA / f)
```

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import lrrcs as lrr
from great_tables import GT

KIKU_GT = dict(table_background_color="transparent",
               table_font_size="0.92rem",
               heading_title_font_size="1.05rem",
               heading_subtitle_font_size="0.85rem",
               source_notes_font_size="0.8rem",
               column_labels_font_weight="bold",
               data_row_padding="4px")

# Everything a claim needs beyond its loading, held fixed across the firms.
BASE = dict(mu=0.0015, phi_sigma=7.5, alpha=0.5)

firms = lrr.LongRunRisksModel(
    claims={"A": dict(BASE, phi=0.5), "B": dict(BASE, phi=1.5)},
    long="B", short="A",
).solve(method="analytical")

names = list(firms.claims)
rows = pd.DataFrame({
    "firm": names,
    "phi": [firms.params.dividends[n].phi for n in names],
    "a1": [firms.A1[n] for n in names],
    "prem": [firms.long_run_premium[n] for n in names],
    "growth": [firms.expected_growth[n] for n in names],
    "gordon": [firms.gordon_return[n] for n in names],
})

(
    GT(rows)
    .tab_header(title="Two firms that differ only in the loading")
    .cols_label(firm="firm", phi="phi", a1="A1", prem="long_run_premium %",
                growth="expected_growth %", gordon="gordon_return %")
    .fmt_number(columns="phi", decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(columns="a1", decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(columns=["prem", "growth", "gordon"], decimals=2)
    .tab_source_note("One analytical solve of a two-claim model on the "
                     "Table II economy.")
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

Firm B's dividends track the persistent component of consumption, so
its price-dividend ratio moves with long-run news ($A_1 = 15.2$) and its
compensation for that news is positive, 0.14 percent a year. Firm A
behaves in the opposite way. Its loading of 0.5 sits below the
household's $1/\psi = 0.67$ threshold from
[Chapter 6](06-log-linear-solution.qmd), so its valuation moves against
the news ($A_1 = -3.0$) and its compensation for $x_t$ news is slightly
negative, $-0.03$ percent. A hedge pays less, because the household
will accept a lower return on a claim that does well precisely when
long-run news is bad.

Now look at the Gordon column. The Gordon formula uses only expected
growth, so it puts the two firms 0.12 points apart (7.01 versus 6.89
percent), which is almost entirely the mechanical difference in
expected growth. The economics of the two rows is in the risk the
Gordon formula omits. `long_run_premium` is the part of that risk that
comes from $x_t$ news, and short-run and volatility news add more.

## Pricing the value and growth legs

Now run the same steps on the 1930 to 2003 data that
[Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd) built. Step 1 uses the
panel's dividend growth series, and step 2 runs the equation (19)
regression. The value leg is missing dividend growth in two depression
years, so the regression masks non-finite pairs, which is the same
arithmetic Chapter 8 ran:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

dc = pl.read_csv(DATA / "consumption_annual.csv").sort("year")["dc"].to_numpy()
panel = pl.read_csv(DATA / "annual_panel.csv")

def dividend_growth(claim):
    return (
        panel.filter(pl.col("claim") == claim)
        .sort("year")["dgrowth"]
        .to_numpy()
    )

ma = lrr.expected_growth_proxy(dc, window=2)

def leverage(dd):
    mask = np.isfinite(ma) & np.isfinite(dd)
    x = ma[mask] - ma[mask].mean()
    e = dd[mask] - dd[mask].mean()
    return float(np.dot(x, e) / np.dot(x, x))

phi = {c: leverage(dividend_growth(c)) for c in ("Value", "Growth", "Market")}
(
    GT(pd.DataFrame({"claim": list(phi), "slope": list(phi.values())}))
    .tab_header(title="Measured long-run leverages")
    .cols_label(claim="", slope="phi_tilde")
    .fmt_number(columns="slope", decimals=2)
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

Value's dividends load heavily on the slow component of consumption,
and growth's barely respond. On the reconstruction here, growth's slope
is even slightly negative, and the market sits in between. For complete
series, `lrr.calibration.calibrate_from_data` wraps the same regression
in one call and also estimates the short-run parameters ($\mu$,
$\phi_\sigma$, $\alpha$):

```{python}
div = lrr.calibration.calibrate_from_data(
    dc,
    frequency="annual",
    window=2,
    short=dividend_growth("Growth"),
    market=dividend_growth("Market"),
)
(
    GT(pd.DataFrame([
        {"portfolio": name, "mu": d.mu, "phi": d.phi,
         "phi_sigma": d.phi_sigma, "alpha": d.alpha}
        for name, d in div.items()
    ]))
    .tab_header(title="Calibrated dividend parameters")
    .cols_label(portfolio="", mu="mu (monthly)", phi="phi (long-run)",
                phi_sigma="phi_sigma", alpha="alpha")
    .fmt_number(columns="mu", decimals=5)
    .fmt_number(columns="phi", decimals=3)
    .fmt_number(columns=["phi_sigma", "alpha"], decimals=2)
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

The slopes match the regression run by hand above. The signature has no
argument for returns, by design, so the Euler equation stays a test
rather than becoming a target. `lrr.LongRunRisksModel.from_cashflows`
runs the same calibration and hands back a model that is ready to
solve.

For steps 3 and 4, put both measured loadings into one model and solve
it. Everything except the loading is held at the same values as the two
synthetic firms above, so the only difference between the rows is the
measured cash-flow exposure. Naming the long leg and the short leg lets
the results object report the spread itself:

```{python}
legs = lrr.LongRunRisksModel(
    claims={"value leg": dict(BASE, phi=phi["Value"]),
            "growth leg": dict(BASE, phi=phi["Growth"])},
    long="value leg", short="growth leg",
).solve(method="analytical")

print(f"Value-growth spread from long-run risks: "
      f"{legs.value_premium:.2f} points")

leg_names = list(legs.claims)
(
    GT(pd.DataFrame({
        "leg": leg_names,
        "phi": [legs.params.dividends[n].phi for n in leg_names],
        "a1": [legs.A1[n] for n in leg_names],
        "prem": [legs.long_run_premium[n] for n in leg_names],
    }))
    .tab_header(title="The two legs priced from measured loadings")
    .cols_label(leg="", phi="phi", a1="A1", prem="long_run_premium %")
    .fmt_number(columns="phi", decimals=2)
    .fmt_number(columns="a1", decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(columns="prem", decimals=2)
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

The premium ordering follows the measured leverage. The leg whose
dividends load on long-run news earns compensation for that risk, and
the leg whose dividends do not earns a small hedge discount. The spread
is positive even though no return ever entered the calculation.

Do not read the level literally. About seventy annual observations are
enough to establish a ranking but not a third decimal. Table VI of the
paper reports annual slopes of $-0.38$ for growth and $2.16$ for value,
where the reconstruction here prints $-0.27$ and $12.13$, so the ranking
survives and the point estimates do not. Moreover, an annual slope is
not the monthly loading the full solution uses (Table II sets
$\phi_V = 6.2$, $\phi_G = 2.6$), and at $\tilde\phi = 12.13$ the
log-linear elasticity of 208.9 comes from applying the formula well
past the region it was linearized for. The demonstration establishes
the ordering and the mechanism, not the decimals.

## When your claim is not a traded portfolio

The steps do not require a traded portfolio, because any cash-flow
growth series can be projected on the consumption moving average.
Outside traded portfolios, though, measurement error and the
linearization anchor deserve extra caution.

First, the loading is measured with error. The regression above had
seven decades of exchange-listed dividends, and the point estimate
still moved from 2.16 to 12.13 across reconstructions. A firm's
distributable earnings over 15 or 20 years measure $\tilde\phi$ with
even more error, so the honest output is a range. Price the claim at
the low and high ends of a confidence band for the loading rather than
at the point estimate.

Second, the anchor is an assumption. A claim the model has no anchor
for linearizes around a mean log price-dividend ratio of 3.30. The
model does not know your claim's actual valuation, and the
`mean_log_pd` attribute of the results repeats the assumption rather
than predicting anything. If your claim's valuation ratio sits far from
$e^{3.30} \approx 27$, the elasticities and the Gordon comparison drift
with it, and you should move the anchor by passing `pd_anchor=` to
`solve`. The sign and
ordering logic survives. A loading above $1/\psi$ means the valuation
rises on good long-run news and the claim owes a premium for it, and a
loading below $1/\psi$ means the opposite.

## Takeaways

- Any claim is priced from one measured number, the loading of its
  cash-flow growth on the two-year moving average of lagged consumption
  growth. Returns never enter, so the premium is a prediction.
- The analytical solve returns the valuation response to growth news
  ($A_1$), the compensation that response commands
  (`long_run_premium`), and the Gordon return, which is the number a
  DCF would report from growth alone, with no adjustment for the risk
  that separates the claims.
- On the 1930 to 2003 data the measured leverages are 12.13 (value),
  $-0.27$ (growth) and 0.72 (market), and the implied premium ordering
  follows the leverage ordering.
- Short samples measure the loading with substantial error, and the
  anchor P/D of 3.30 is a linearization point, not a fitted level.
  Trust the ordering and the sign, and do not trust the third decimal.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recall"}

Answer from memory before opening.

1. What single measured number does your claim contribute, and how is
   it measured?
2. The analytical solve returns three numbers for your claim. Name
   them, and say which one a DCF of the same claim would have reported.
3. Why should you trust the ordering of your results and not the third
   decimal?

**Answers.**

1. The loading of its cash-flow growth on the two-year moving average
   of lagged consumption growth.
2. The valuation response $A_1$, the compensation
   `long_run_premium`, and the Gordon return. A DCF would have shown
   only the Gordon return.
3. Short samples measure the loading with substantial error, and the
   anchor P/D is a linearization point, not a fitted level.

:::

## Exercises

1. Price a claim with $\phi = 0.67$ (the household's $1/\psi$). Confirm
   `A1` and `long_run_premium` are approximately zero, and explain why
   the threshold is $1/\psi$ rather than 0.
2. Re-run the equation (19) regression with `window=3` in
   `expected_growth_proxy`. Does the value-growth leverage ranking
   survive? Compare with exercise 1 of
   [Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd).
3. Drop 1930 to 1945 from the sample and re-estimate $\tilde\phi$ for
   both legs, then re-price them. How much does the spread move, and
   what does the answer tell you about which years supply the
   identifying variation?
4. Take any dividend-paying portfolio you can build a yearly
   dividend-growth series for, run the four steps, and write down the
   loading, the premium, and the Gordon return. Which of the three
   numbers would a DCF valuation of the same portfolio have shown you?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
# Exercise 1: the riskless long-run loading
res0 = lrr.LongRunRisksModel.from_loading(1 / 1.5).solve(method="analytical")
print(f"phi = 1/psi = {1/1.5:.3f}:  A1 = {res0.A1['claim']:.3f}, "
      f"long-run premium = {res0.long_run_premium['claim']:+.3f} %/yr")

# Exercise 2: a different proxy window
ma3 = lrr.expected_growth_proxy(dc, window=3)
def leverage_on(dd, proxy):
    mask = np.isfinite(proxy) & np.isfinite(dd)
    x = proxy[mask] - proxy[mask].mean()
    e = dd[mask] - dd[mask].mean()
    return float(np.dot(x, e) / np.dot(x, x))
for c in ("Value", "Growth"):
    print(f"{c:6s}  window 2: {phi[c]:7.2f}"
          f"   window 3: {leverage_on(dividend_growth(c), ma3):7.2f}")

# Exercise 3: dropping 1930-1945
years_c = (pl.read_csv(DATA / "consumption_annual.csv").sort("year")
           ["year"].to_numpy())
keep = years_c >= 1946
ma_post = lrr.expected_growth_proxy(dc[keep], window=2)
prem = {}
for c in ("Value", "Growth"):
    dd_post = (panel.filter(pl.col("claim") == c)
               .filter(pl.col("year") >= 1946).sort("year")
               ["dgrowth"].to_numpy())
    lev = leverage_on(dd_post, ma_post)
    prem[c] = (lrr.LongRunRisksModel.from_loading(lev)
               .solve(method="analytical").long_run_premium["claim"])
    print(f"{c:6s}  post-war phi: {lev:7.2f}   premium: {prem[c]:+.2f} %/yr")
print(f"post-war spread: {prem['Value'] - prem['Growth']:.2f} points")
```

At the household's own loading the claim is long-run riskless, so both the
elasticity and the premium are zero. The threshold is 1/psi rather than 0
because a claim growing with expected consumption moves exactly as the
household's consumption does. The window change is not innocuous. At window 3 the value slope turns
negative, the same fragility the Chapter 8 check showed, so treat the
level of any single-window leverage estimate with caution. The pre-war years carry a large share of the identifying
variation, so the post-war slopes and the spread shrink, a warning about
how much data the loading estimates need.

Exercise 4 is yours. Run the four steps on a series you bring, and note
that a DCF of the same portfolio would have shown you only the Gordon
return, never the loading or the premium decomposition.
